subject: Uptime accounting: DNS maintenance handshake vs partial degradation
messages:
From: ACME Platform <sre@acmeretail.com>
To: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 5 Oct 2026 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: Observed partial degradation 10/05 — asking for SLA attribution

Hi Sean,

We observed an increase in 5xxs and DNS resolution latency for ACME storefronts between 2026-10-05T14:07:00Z and 2026-10-05T14:28:00Z. Our telemetry indicates a sharp spike in origin connect failures that correlate with DNS failures from BlueWave. We saw ~11% error rate for that 21-minute window leading to measurable page load failures.

ACME has been calculating this as a Redwood availability event. BlueWave told us they were doing a short maintenance handshake at 14:10Z but claim it was completed in under a minute. Given the user impact we need clarity on how Redwood attributes uptime when an upstream DNS provider performs a maintenance handshake that increases client-side latency but doesn't fully return SERVFAILs for the entire window.

Please advise next steps — we need an initial assessment and whether we'll be eligible for SLA credit, plus any logs/evidence required.

Thanks,
Sam R.
Senior SRE, ACME Retail

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 6 Oct 2026 11:42:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Observed partial degradation 10/05 — internal analysis

Sean / Grace — I finished an initial correlation between our edge probes, the ACME traces, and BlueWave logs. Key findings below: 

- Timeline (UTC):
  - 14:07:12Z — first observable uptick in DNS resolution latency across 6 edge probes (median jump from 30ms to 220ms).
  - 14:09:48Z — BlueWave reports TSIG rotation start.
  - 14:11:03Z — BlueWave rotation end.
  - 14:12:10Z — ACME saw highest 5xx spike; downstream retries and cache misses contributed to the user-visible error rate.

- Root cause analysis: BlueWave's TSIG rotation caused transient elevated DNS latency and a small SERVFAIL tail. However, because our routers continued to attempt origin connections and our KV cache had a 12% miss rate during 14:09—14:13Z, the user impact was extended beyond BlueWave's 75s window. In short: primary trigger was third-party maintenance, but our caching/connection retry behavior amplified the duration of user impact.

- Attribution guidance (draft):
  - Per SLA, events caused exclusively by an upstream provider are typically excluded.
  - In this case, BlueWave triggered the initial disruption, but Redwood’s cache expiry/eviction and retry/backoff policy contributed materially to the extended impact window.
  - Proposal: apportion the 21-minute window between BlueWave (first 1.5 minutes) and Redwood (remaining ~19.5 minutes) for the purposes of calculating credits. We would present ACME with a proportional credit calculation reflecting Redwood's partial responsibility.

Next steps: I can prepare a concise evidence package (edge probe pcap + cache eviction summary + BlueWave logs) for ACME and a suggested credit math. Grace, once you confirm BlueWave's timestamps fully align, I’ll finalize.

—Rishi
SRE, Redwood Inference

From: Sean Gallagher <sean_gallagher@redwood.ai>
To: Sam R. <sre@acmeretail.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai>, Maya Patel <ops@bluewave.net>
Date: Thu, 8 Oct 2026 09:22:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: Observed partial degradation 10/05 — proposed attribution and next steps

Hi Sam — thanks for flagging this. We completed an internal analysis and coordinated with BlueWave. Short summary and proposal below.

What happened
- BlueWave performed a TSIG rotation/cluster handshake between 2026-10-05T14:09:48Z and 2026-10-05T14:11:03Z which caused an initial spike in DNS latency and a small number of SERVFAILs (BlueWave logs attached).
- That short disturbance propagated: our edge layer experienced elevated DNS resolution times and our KV/response caches saw increased misses, which lengthened ACME's user-impact window to ~21 minutes (14:07Z—14:28Z).

Proposed attribution and credit approach
- We agree BlueWave's maintenance was the initiating cause. Per Redwood SLA language, events caused solely by upstream providers are excluded. However, because Redwood's cache expiry and retry behavior materially extended the incident, we propose a shared attribution model:
  - BlueWave: 2 minutes credited to upstream maintenance window (their 75s rotation + conservative padding).
  - Redwood: remaining 19 minutes — we acknowledge partial responsibility.

Credit computation (example)
- ACME has a monthly uptime SLO of 99.95%. For the affected billing month this 21-minute degradation equates to X% of the available minutes. Based on proportional attribution, Redwood would apply a pro-rated credit for the 19-minute portion. We will provide the exact credit calculation as a follow-up (requires billing window alignment).

Evidence package
- Attached: bluewave-dns-incident-logs.zip, redwood-probe-traces-10-05.pcap, redwood-cache-summary-1005.csv.

Operational changes
- Rishi has already proposed short-term mitigations: (1) adjust resolver retry/backoff at the edge for 60s after probe-detected upstream maintenance, (2) increase short-term cache TTLs for known high-churn records for customers that opt-in. We’ll share a rollout plan for these controls.

Next steps
1) Sam — confirm ACME wants Redwood to apply a pro-rated credit for the 19-minute allocation (and confirm which billing month to apply it to).
2) If accepted, Redwood will calculate the exact credit amount and issue a credit memo.
3) We will coordinate with BlueWave on process improvements and request formal postmortem entries into BW ticket #BW-1138.

Apologies for the user impact — we want to be transparent and fair here. Happy to hop on a quick call this week to walk through evidence and the math.

Best,
Sean Gallagher
Head of Customer Escalations, Redwood Inference
